turns.user: i want to start meal prepping on sundays, work gets crazy and i end up ordering food like 4 nights a week. one person, i have a decent oven and a rice cooker. how do i actually do it
turns.assistant:
Here's a simple routine that takes about 2 hours on Sunday:

1. **Pick a plan before shopping.** Choose 1 protein, 1 grain, 2 vegetables, and 1 sauce for the week. For example: baked chicken thighs, rice, roasted broccoli, roasted sweet potato, and a peanut or teriyaki sauce.
2. **Shop once** with that list.
3. **Start the slow things first:** put the rice in the rice cooker and the chicken and sweet potatoes in the oven at 425F (they can share trays).
4. **While those cook,** wash and chop the raw veg, make the sauce, and roast the broccoli on a second tray once the first comes out.
5. **Cool everything** for about 20 minutes, then portion into 4 or 5 containers.
6. **Refrigerate** meals for Monday to Thursday and freeze the rest for Friday onward.

The point is to cook components, not full recipes, so you can mix them differently.

turns.user: ok but wont it get boring eating the same thing 5 days
turns.assistant:
It can, which is why most people who stick with prep make components rather than five identical meals. Use the same base but vary the sauce and the format:

- Day 1: chicken, rice and broccoli with teriyaki
- Day 2: chicken in a burrito bowl with salsa and beans
- Day 3: chicken and sweet potato in a wrap with hummus
- Day 4: fried rice with the leftover rice and an egg

Keep two or three different sauces or spice mixes in the fridge. Fresh toppings like avocado, cheese, pickles or hot sauce added at mealtime make a big difference. You can also prep two proteins instead of one, like chicken and a pot of chili, and alternate.

turns.user: how long does cooked chicken and rice actually last in the fridge? i dont wanna get sick
turns.assistant:
The standard food safety guidance is 3 to 4 days for cooked chicken and cooked rice in the fridge at 40F (4C) or below. Rice needs a bit more care: cool it quickly (spread it on a tray or divide into containers soon after cooking) and get it in the fridge within an hour or so, because Bacillus cereus spores can survive cooking and grow at room temperature.

For a 5-day week, I'd keep meals for Monday through Wednesday or Thursday in the fridge and freeze the rest in individual containers, then move Friday's meal to the fridge Thursday night to thaw. Reheat until steaming hot all the way through.

turns.user: makes sense. what containers should i get
turns.assistant:
Glass containers with snap lids are the best all-round choice: they go in the microwave and oven, don't stain or hold smells, and last for years. Pyrex or Snapware 3-cup or 4-cup sizes work well for one-person meals.

If weight matters because you carry lunch to work, a few BPA-free plastic containers are lighter. Get ones labeled microwave safe. Look for ones with a divided compartment if you hate things mixing, though sauces in a small separate container are better.

Buy 8 to 10 to start so you have enough for the fridge and freezer. Masking tape and a marker to label dates is cheap and helps you track what's older.

turns.user: im starting gre prep, taking it in 3 months. can someone explain how the scoring works, like whats the adaptive thing. is it per question or what
turns.assistant:
The GRE General Test is adaptive by section, not by question. For both Verbal and Quant, you get two sections. Your performance on the first section determines the difficulty of the second. If you do well on the first, you get a harder second section, which has a higher scoring ceiling; if you do less well, you get an easier one.

Within a section you can skip around, change answers and go back, which is different from tests that adapt after every question. Your score on each of Verbal and Quant is scaled to 130 to 170 in 1-point steps, and Analytical Writing is scored 0 to 6 in half-point steps.

The scaled score takes into account the number of correct answers and the difficulty of the questions you saw.

turns.user: so if i get the harder section but miss a bunch is that worse than the easier one
turns.assistant:
Not necessarily. The harder section is worth more per correct answer, so even if you miss several you can end up with a higher score than someone who got nearly everything right in the easier section. It's roughly the case that someone who gets the hard second section can reach 170, while the easy section caps out lower, around 160 or so, even with a perfect section.

So you want to do well on the first section to be routed to the hard one, but you shouldn't panic if the second section feels tough. That feeling usually means you're on the harder path, which is a good sign.

turns.user: ok and how do they actually decide which questions are hard? like who decides
turns.assistant:
ETS pretests questions. Experimental questions are mixed into the exam (one unscored section) and test-takers answer them. ETS then uses statistics on how many people answer each question correctly, and which kinds of test-takers do, to estimate difficulty. A question that most high-scorers get right and low-scorers get wrong is rated differently from one that everyone misses.

This is based on item response theory, a statistical model that gives each question a difficulty value and a measure of how well it separates stronger and weaker test-takers. Questions are also reviewed by content experts to make sure they fit the intended skills and are fair.

turns.user: wait theres an unscored section? how do i know which one
turns.assistant:
You can't know. The unscored (experimental) section can be in Verbal or Quant and it looks exactly like a real one. Sometimes you also get an unidentified research section at the end of the test. Because of this, you should treat every section as if it counts.

For the test day you'll typically see: Analytical Writing, then Verbal and Quant sections in varying order, with a 10-minute break after the third section. If you see three sections of the same type, one of them is the experimental one, but you still won't know which.

turns.user: annoying lol. last q does the order of verbal vs quant matter
turns.assistant:
The order doesn't change how scoring works, but it can affect your performance. Quant and Verbal can come in either order after the writing task, and you can't choose it for the at-home or test center versions. So practice both orders.

If you're stronger in one area, simulating the case where your weaker section comes first, when you're freshest, is useful. Take full-length practice tests in one sitting, with the same timing as the real test, to train your stamina. The test is about 2 hours long in the current shortened format, so stamina matters less than it used to, but the practice still helps.

turns.user: helping my kid with physics hw and i forgot everything. a block slides down a frictionless ramp, 30 degrees, 2 m long. do i use energy conservation or newtons laws to find speed at the bottom? which is easier
turns.assistant:
Energy conservation is quicker here. Both give the same answer.

Energy: the block loses height h = 2 sin30 = 1 m. All the lost potential energy becomes kinetic, so mgh = 1/2 mv^2, and v = sqrt(2gh) = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 1) = about 4.43 m/s. The mass cancels out.

Newton's laws: acceleration along the ramp is g sin30 = 4.9 m/s^2. Then use v^2 = 2as = 2 x 4.9 x 2 = 19.6, so v = 4.43 m/s.

Newton works too, but needs two steps (find a, then use a kinematics equation). Energy is one step when you only want the speed and not the time.

turns.user: ok and if the question asks for how long it takes then? do i need newton for that
turns.assistant:
Yes, for time you'll need the kinematics side. Energy doesn't tell you anything about time.

Using the acceleration a = 4.9 m/s^2, you can use s = 1/2 a t^2, so t = sqrt(2s/a) = sqrt(4/4.9) = about 0.90 s. Or use v = at, with v = 4.43, so t = 4.43/4.9 = 0.90 s.

So for this ramp, use energy for the speed, then Newton or kinematics for the time. If the problem has friction, both approaches still work but you add the friction force (or the work done by friction in the energy equation).

turns.user: what if theres friction, which method is better then
turns.assistant:
With friction both still work, and energy is still usually a bit easier if you only want the final speed.

Energy with friction: mgh minus the work done by friction equals 1/2 mv^2. Friction force is mu x mg cos(theta), and the work is that force times the distance along the ramp.

Newton with friction: acceleration is g(sin theta - mu cos theta), then use kinematics for the speed and time.

In practice Newton's method is cleaner when friction is involved, because the acceleration is constant and you can get everything from one formula. Energy is cleaner when the path is curved or complicated. For a straight ramp with friction either is fine. Pick whichever matches what your kid's class is working on right now.

turns.user: I'm going to Lisbon for a week in May for a client meeting plus a few days of sightseeing, and I can't decide between taking a carry-on only or checking a bag. I usually bring a lot of gear (laptop, sketchbook, camera). What would you suggest?

Lisbon also has steep, cobbled streets, so a light bag is much easier to manage.

Checking a bag makes sense if you have to bring bulky items, such as a tripod or multiple lenses, or if you plan to shop and bring back purchases. Your camera, laptop and sketchbook should travel in the cabin regardless, since you don't want to check electronics.

So the question is what else you're packing. If clothing for a week fits in a 40L carry-on with your laptop in a separate personal item, go carry-on.

The 38L duffel is lighter, squishes into tight overhead bins, and you can carry it on your shoulder or back if it has straps. Its drawbacks are that it offers less structure, so clothes crease more, and a heavy shoulder bag gets tiring.
